name: Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport
before:
Nigeria's capital airport, about 20 km south west of central Abuja. There are separate international and domestic terminals but they share a single runway, which is the detail that matters most here.

That runway has form. In 2017 it had been in service nearly forty years against a twenty year design life and was showing real fatigue, so the government closed the airport for six weeks and diverted flights to Kaduna while Julius Berger rebuilt it. It reopened on 17 April 2017, two days early.

The terminal arrangement is straightforward. The building opened in 2002 handles international flights and the older one alongside it takes domestic.

There is a private jet wing serving business, diplomatic and political traffic, with a dedicated general aviation terminal planned.

Both the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority and the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau have their head offices on the airport. It is named after Nnamdi Azikiwe, Nigeria's first president.
after:
Nnamdi Azikiwe International is Abuja's airport, west of the city.

It has a single runway, which is the detail that matters most here. By 2017 the runway had long outlived its 20-year design life, and the airport closed for six weeks from 8 March while Julius Berger rebuilt it, with flights diverted to Kaduna. The work finished on 17 April 2017, two days ahead of schedule.

A new terminal, built to handle 15 million passengers a year, was commissioned in December 2018.

The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority and the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau both have their head offices at the airport.
